title: Finding roots: bisection, false position, Newton, secant
subtitle: Most equations cannot be solved with algebra. Numerical methods creep up on the answer instead, and they differ enormously in how fast.

sections.title: The problem and the errors
sections.body:
Try solving x³ − x − 2 = 0 with the tricks you learned at school. Go on, I’ll wait. You won’t find a neat formula, and the same is true for cos x = x. Most real equations have no tidy answer, so we do something cleverer: we sneak up on the root.

Step one is locating a root. If f is continuous and f(a), f(b) have opposite signs, a root lies between them (the intermediate value theorem), because the graph must cross the axis to get from below to above. Step two is refining by iteration. Two errors matter: the truncation error of the method and the round-off error of the machine; accuracy is often stated as the tolerance at which iteration stops. Test f(x) = x³ − x − 2: f(1) = −2 and f(2) = 4. Opposite signs, so a root lies in [1, 2].

worked.why: f(x) = x³ − x − 2. Test f(1) and f(2).
Opposite signs, so a root lies in [1, 2].

questions.prompt: f(1) = −2 and f(2) = 4 for continuous f. What follows?

keynotes: Most equations, such as x³ − x − 2 = 0 or cos x = x, have no formula, so we locate a root and refine it by iteration.
If f is continuous and f(a), f(b) have opposite signs, a root lies between them (intermediate value theorem); here f(1) = −2 and f(2) = 4 put a root in [1, 2].
Two errors matter: the truncation error of the method and the round-off error of the machine; iteration stops at a tolerance.

sections.title: Bisection
sections.body:
Guess a number between 1 and 100 and I’ll say “higher” or “lower”. You would pick 50, then 25 or 75, halving each time. That is bisection. Take the midpoint c; keep the half whose ends still have opposite signs. Each step halves the interval: after n steps the error is ≤ (b − a)/2ⁿ. It is guaranteed to converge, but slowly, gaining one binary digit per step.

For x³ − x − 2 on [1, 2] it reaches 1.5214 in 21 iterations to tolerance 10⁻⁶. How many steps do you need in theory? From an interval of length 1 you want 1/2ⁿ < 10⁻⁶, so n > log₂(10⁶) ≈ 19.9, that is 20 iterations. The violet lines in the figure mark the shrinking bracket.

worked.why: Iterations needed to get within 10⁻⁶ from an interval of length 1.

sections.title: False position (regula falsi)
sections.body:
Bisection is polite but, as you may have noticed, it ignores information: it never asks how big f is at the ends. If f(a) is tiny and f(b) is huge, the root is surely nearer a. False position (regula falsi) uses that. Draw the chord between (a, f(a)) and (b, f(b)) and take where it crosses the axis: c = (a·f(b) − b·f(a)) / (f(b) − f(a)). Keep the sub-interval with the sign change, as in bisection.

Because it uses the size of f, it is usually faster (13 iterations here), though one end can stay stuck for a convex function. Each point in the figure is where a chord meets the axis. False position differs from bisection in that it uses the function values, not just their signs.

choices.text: Does not need a sign change.
Picks the point where the secant line crosses zero rather than the midpoint.

sections.title: Newton–Raphson
sections.body:
Now for the fastest idea in the chapter, and you will enjoy it. From a guess xₙ, draw the tangent to f and let it hit the axis: xn+1 = xₙ − f(xₙ)/f′(xₙ). Near a simple root the convergence is quadratic: the number of correct digits roughly doubles each step. The price: it needs f′, a good start, and it fails where f′ ≈ 0.

Find √2 from x₀ = 1 using f = x² − 2, f′ = 2x. x₁ = 1 − (1 − 2)/2 = 1.5, then x₂ = 1.5 − (2.25 − 2)/3 = 1.41667. It takes 5 iterations to 10⁻⁹; x³ − x − 2 from 1.5 takes 3. In the figure the residuals collapse: 10⁻¹, 10⁻³, 10⁻⁷… Quadratic convergence means the error is roughly squared at every step.

questions.prompt: Quadratic convergence of Newton’s method means…

choices.text: The error is roughly squared each step (digits double).

problems.prompt: Use Newton’s method on f(x) = x² − 2 from x₀ = 1 for two steps.

keynotes: Newton–Raphson draws the tangent and lets it hit the axis: x(n+1) = xₙ − f(xₙ)/f′(xₙ).
Near a simple root convergence is quadratic: the number of correct digits roughly doubles each step; it needs f′, a good start and fails where f′ ≈ 0.
Finding √2 from x₀ = 1 gives 1.5 then 1.41667 and takes 5 iterations to 10⁻⁹; x³ − x − 2 from 1.5 takes 3.

sections.title: Secant method
sections.body:
What if computing the derivative is hard or impossible? Replace f′ by the slope through the last two points, and you get the secant method: xn+1 = xₙ − f(xₙ)(xₙ − xn−1)/(f(xₙ) − f(xn−1)). You need no derivative and no bracket, just two starting guesses; the order of convergence is ≈ 1.618.

Here it takes 7 iterations. Compare the four methods on the same equation in the figures: they all land on the root ≈ 1.5214, just at different speeds. The secant method needs two starting guesses, no derivative.

choices.text: Two starting values but no derivative.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: The slope is estimated from the last two iterates.

figures.caption: Figure 1.5.1 — secant
figures.note: Two starting guesses, no bracket needed.

keynotes: The secant method replaces f′ by the slope through the last two points and needs no derivative and no bracket, only two starting guesses.
Here it takes 7 iterations and finds the root ≈ 1.5214.

sections.title: Choosing a method
sections.body:
Which method should you pick? There is no single winner, so here is the full comparison in one place.

MethodNeedsOrderGuaranteed?
Bisectionbracket1 (linear, ½)yes
False positionbracket≥ 1yes
Newtonf, f′, good guess2no
Secanttwo guesses1.618no

Practical recipe: bracket with bisection until close, then finish with Newton. Slow and safe first, fast and risky last. Which method is certain to converge if you have a bracket? Bisection (and false position).

questions.prompt: Which method is certain to converge if you have a bracket?

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Newton and secant can diverge or jump away.

keynotes: Bisection and false position need a bracket and are guaranteed to converge.
Newton (order 2) needs f, f′ and a good guess; the secant method (order 1.618) needs two guesses; neither is guaranteed.
Practical recipe: bracket with bisection until close, then finish with Newton.
